Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder at kodely.me).

BUILD: an admin CMS for the blog / SEO pages.

## Why this is urgent, not cosmetic
**56 posts are live on kodely.me right now and some of them are wrong.** Two known problems:
1. Batch-1 posts state *"A typical first build runs roughly 100–150 credits."* Real measurements are 144 and 472 — the second is over 3x the top of that range.
2. Several say *"there's no zip or full-project download."* True today, but `app/api/projects/[id]/export/route.ts` is built and pending deploy, which inverts it.

Right now the ONLY way to fix live content is a seed script run on the production box. There is no way for a human to read what is published, search it, or correct a sentence. That is why this matters.

## Read first
- `prisma/schema.prisma` → `BlogPost` (slug, title, metaDescription, category, targetKeyword, bodyHtml, publishedAt, updatedAt). **READ ONLY — do not change the schema.**
- `app/blog/page.tsx` and `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` — the render contract. `bodyHtml` goes through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` with **no sanitisation and no wrapper**, so malformed markup breaks a live page's layout. `.article-body` styles only a fixed set of tags — check exactly which. The post page renders `title` as the only `<h1>`.
- `scripts/seo/validate.mjs` — a validator with 20+ checks already exists. **Reuse its rules; do not write a second, divergent set.** If you cannot import it directly from a server component, say so and explain what you did instead.
- `app/admin/users/page.tsx` for query patterns and visual idiom; `lib/auth.ts` for `getAdminUser()`.

## Build
1. **List** — every post: title, slug, category, published date, last updated. Searchable by title/slug/body, filterable by category, paginated. **Flag posts whose body matches known-stale patterns** (a credit figure, "no zip or full-project download", "Not yet" in an export row) — that turns this page into the tool that fixes the live-content problem rather than just a viewer.
2. **Edit** — title, metaDescription, category, targetKeyword, bodyHtml. **Validate before saving** and refuse to save invalid HTML, for the reason above: unsanitised markup goes straight onto a public page.
3. **Preview** — let an admin see the rendered result before publishing the change.
4. `getAdminUser()` at the top of every page, `notFound()` if null.

## Critical constraints
- **`bodyHtml` is the dangerous field.** It is injected unsanitised into a public page. Only an authenticated ADMIN may write it — never widen that. Validate structure (balanced tags, allowed tag set, no `<script>`, no external `src`/`href` to remote hosts, no `<h1>`) on the server, not just in the browser.
- **Do not bulk-edit or auto-fix anything.** Surface the stale posts; let a human decide each one. An automated find-and-replace across 56 live pages is exactly how a small error becomes 56 errors.
- YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT: `app/admin/content/**`.
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything under lib/, app/api/**, app/blog/**, other app/admin/** subtrees, scripts/**, content/**, app/globals.css, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- Match the admin visual idiom (`rounded-xl border border-black/10 dark:border-white/10`, `text-sm`, monochrome). No new white-on-brand-gradient text (fails contrast — known accepted issue). Real labels, visible `focus-visible:` states.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components` must BOTH be clean.** Parallel agents are running — errors in files you did not touch are not yours.
- Local Postgres has 17 posts. You may edit and revert your own test changes; **do not leave any post modified**. Record the original values before you touch anything.

## Report back
What you built, how you reused the validator, which stale-content patterns you flag and how many local posts match, what you verified, and confirmation that no post was left modified.

40	// coordination point for admin surfaces owned by other people. So names are
41	// admitted here only when the SURFACE ALREADY EXISTS in the tree, and each one
42	// records whether anything actually emits it (ADMIN_ACTION_INFO). Two do today;
43	// the rest are a work order, and /admin/audit renders the outstanding list from
44	// that data — so it stays visible long after this comment stops being read.

66	 * The panel area an action happens in. Fifteen dotted strings in one flat list
67	 * is a vocabulary you have to already know to use; the same fifteen under six
68	 * headings is one you can read. This exists so /admin/audit can group its
69	 * filter and its outstanding-work list without hard-coding a second copy of the
70	 * vocabulary in the page — the module owns what the names MEAN, the page owns
71	 * how they look.
72	 *
73	 * Ordered roughly by how much customer data the area exposes.
74	 */
75	export const ADMIN_SURFACES = ["customers", "sites", "support", "dashboard", "flags", "audit"] as const;

80	  customers: "Customers",
81	  sites: "Published sites",
82	  support: "Feedback & support notes",
83	  dashboard: "Cost dashboard",
84	  flags: "Feature flags",
85	  audit: "Audit log",

89	 * Read or write. Not decoration: an unrecorded WRITE is strictly worse than an
90	 * unrecorded read — it means state changed and nothing anywhere says who
91	 * changed it — so this is what sorts the outstanding list on /admin/audit, and
92	 * it is the first cut anyone makes when reading the log ("what actually
93	 * changed?" before "who looked?").
94	 */

99	  note: string;
100	  kind: AdminActionKind;
101	  surface: AdminSurface;
102	  emittedBy: string | null;
103	};

107	 *
108	 * `emittedBy: null` means the surface exists and reads or writes without
109	 * recording anything. That is not a footnote: it is a live gap in the record,
110	 * and holding it as data rather than prose is what lets /admin/audit show the
111	 * outstanding list instead of a comment nobody opens.
112	 *
113	 * Row COUNT cannot substitute for this. `site.taken_down` has a real emitter
114	 * and will sit at zero rows for months, because taking a site down is rare —
115	 * "no rows" and "nothing is watching" are different conditions and a panel that
116	 * conflated them would cry wolf until people stopped reading it.
117	 *
118	 * Keyed by the union, so adding a name without saying where it comes from is a
119	 * type error rather than a blank cell.
120	 */
121	export const ADMIN_ACTION_INFO: Record<AdminAction, AdminActionInfo> = {
122	  "site.taken_down": {

128	    emittedBy: "app/admin/sites/actions.ts",

154	    kind: "read",

230	/** One action name and everything the vocabulary knows about it. */
231	export type AdminActionDescriptor = AdminActionInfo & { action: AdminAction };
232	
233	function describe(action: AdminAction): AdminActionDescriptor {
234	  return { action, ...ADMIN_ACTION_INFO[action] };
235	}
236	
237	/** Every name in the vocabulary, in declaration order. */
238	export function adminActionDescriptors(): AdminActionDescriptor[] {
239	  return (Object.keys(ADMIN_ACTION_INFO) as AdminAction[]).map(describe);
240	}
241	
242	/**
243	 * The vocabulary as the panel groups it: surfaces in ADMIN_SURFACES order,
244	 * actions in declaration order within each. Surfaces with no actions are
245	 * dropped rather than rendered empty.
246	 */
247	export function adminActionsBySurface(): {
248	  surface: AdminSurface;
249	  label: string;
250	  actions: AdminActionDescriptor[];
251	}[] {
252	  return ADMIN_SURFACES.map((surface) => ({
253	    surface,
254	    label: ADMIN_SURFACE_LABELS[surface],
255	    actions: adminActionDescriptors().filter((d) => d.surface === surface),
256	  })).filter((g) => g.actions.length > 0);
257	}
258	
259	/**
260	 * Actions whose surface exists but records nothing. Empty is the goal.
261	 *
262	 * Writes first: a write nobody records means state changed with no trace of who
263	 * changed it, which is a worse hole than an unrecorded read and should be the
264	 * first thing anyone reads off the panel.
265	 */
266	export function pendingAdminActions(): AdminActionDescriptor[] {
267	  const pending = adminActionDescriptors().filter((d) => d.emittedBy === null);
268	  return [
269	    ...pending.filter((d) => d.kind === "write"),
270	    ...pending.filter((d) => d.kind === "read"),
271	  ];
272	}
273	
274	export function isAdminAction(v: unknown): v is AdminAction {
275	  // hasOwnProperty, not `in`: `in` walks the prototype chain, so `?action=
276	  // toString` would pass a guard whose entire job is to say this name is one of
277	  // OURS — and the caller would then read a Function off ADMIN_ACTION_INFO.
278	  return typeof v === "string" && Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(ADMIN_ACTION_INFO, v);
279	}
280	
281	/**
282	 * What the vocabulary knows about a raw action string, or null if it knows
283	 * nothing. Rows are read back from a plain String column, so this — not a cast
284	 * — is how the page turns one into a label.
285	 */
286	export function describeAdminAction(action: string): AdminActionDescriptor | null {
287	  return isAdminAction(action) ? describe(action) : null;
288	}
289	
290	/**
291	 * What a row can point at. Closed for the same reason the action names are:
292	 * `targetType` is indexed, it is what "everything anyone did to this account"
293	 * filters on, and two spellings of "user" would split that answer in half —
294	 * silently, and in the direction of showing less than happened.
295	 *
296	 * A moderation finding is addressed as its project (with the finding id in
297	 * meta) rather than getting a type of its own: findings have no page, and the
298	 * question people ask is "what has been done to this site".
299	 */
300	export const ADMIN_TARGET_TYPES = {
301	  user: "user",
302	  project: "project",
303	  /** Keyed by the flag's `key`, which is FeatureFlag's primary key. */
304	  flag: "flag",
305	} as const;
306	
307	export type AdminTargetType = (typeof ADMIN_TARGET_TYPES)[keyof typeof ADMIN_TARGET_TYPES];
308	
309	/**
310	 * Flat by design — no nested objects, no arrays. The type is the enforcement:
311	 * you cannot spread a whole Prisma row into it by accident, which is the usual
312	 * way a log like this ends up holding a copy of the data it was meant to guard.
313	 */
314	export type AdminAuditMeta = Record<string, string | number | boolean | null | undefined>;
315	
316	/** Just enough of the admin to attribute the row. `getAdminUser()` satisfies it. */
317	export type AdminActor = { id: string; email: string };
318	
319	/**
320	 * Record one admin action.
321	 *
322	 * ── AWAITED, AND IT THROWS. Deliberately unlike `track()` in lib/events.ts. ──
323	 *
324	 * `track()` is fire-and-forget because a dropped analytics event is a small gap
325	 * in a chart and nobody would trade a failed generation for it. The trade here
326	 * runs the other way: a dropped audit row is a gap in an accountability record,
327	 * and a record with silent gaps is worse than no record at all, because people
328	 * will reason from its absences ("there is no row, so nobody looked").
329	 *
330	 * Two consequences follow, and both are intended:
331	 *
332	 *  1. CALL IT BEFORE THE READ, NOT AFTER. Awaiting the insert before the
333	 *     queries that fetch customer data means there is no window in which an
334	 *     admin has the data and the log does not have the row. `after()` from
335	 *     next/server would keep the page marginally faster and is the right tool
336	 *     for analytics, but it runs once the response is already on the wire —
337	 *     precisely the ordering an audit log must not have.
338	 *  2. A FAILED WRITE FAILS THE PAGE. No swallowed catch. If we cannot record
339	 *     the access, we do not serve the access: the page 500s and the customer
340	 *     data is never rendered. The cost of that posture is small in practice —
341	 *     the same Postgres serves the page's own queries, so an audit write that
342	 *     fails has almost certainly taken the page down anyway — and the failure
343	 *     is loud instead of leaving a hole nobody finds until it matters.
344	 *
345	 * The latency is one INSERT on an internal panel with a handful of users.
346	 */
347	export async function recordAdminAction(
348	  actor: AdminActor,
349	  action: AdminAction,
350	  opts: AdminActionTarget = {},
351	): Promise<void> {
352	  await db.adminAuditLog.create({ data: adminActionRow(actor, action, opts) });
353	}
354	
355	export type AdminActionTarget = {
356	  targetType?: AdminTargetType;
357	  targetId?: string;
358	  meta?: AdminAuditMeta;
359	};
360	
361	/**
362	 * The same row, as data, for the case `recordAdminAction` cannot serve: a write
363	 * that must be ATOMIC with the mutation it records.
364	 *
365	 *   await db.$transaction([
366	 *     db.project.update({ where: { id }, data: { publishedAt: null } }),
367	 *     db.adminAuditLog.create({
368	 *       data: adminActionRow(admin, ADMIN_ACTIONS.siteTakenDown, { ... }),
369	 *     }),
370	 *   ]);
371	 *
372	 * That is strictly stronger than awaiting the helper first — the site cannot go
373	 * dark without the row, and the row cannot exist for a takedown that rolled
374	 * back. Use this inside a transaction and `recordAdminAction` everywhere else;
375	 * either way the action name and target type stay type-checked, which is the
376	 * part a hand-written `db.adminAuditLog.create` gives up.
377	 */
378	export function adminActionRow(
379	  actor: AdminActor,
380	  action: AdminAction,
381	  opts: AdminActionTarget = {},
382	): Prisma.AdminAuditLogUncheckedCreateInput {
383	  return {
384	    actorId: actor.id,
385	    // Denormalised on purpose: the schema keeps actorId as a plain string so
386	    // the row outlives the admin's account, and an id alone would then be
387	    // unreadable. This is the email AS IT WAS at the time of the action.
388	    actorEmail: actor.email,
389	    action,
390	    targetType: opts.targetType ?? null,
391	    targetId: opts.targetId ?? null,
392	    meta: opts.meta ? (JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(opts.meta)) as object) : undefined,
393	  };
394	}
395	
396	// ── Reads ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
397	// The log is only worth writing if it is readable. Queries live here rather
398	// than in the page for the same reason the funnel queries live in
399	// lib/events.ts: the shape of the table is this module's business.
400	
401	export type AdminAuditEntry = {
402	  id: string;
403	  createdAt: Date;
404	  actorId: string;
405	  actorEmail: string;
406	  action: string;
407	  targetType: string | null;
408	  targetId: string | null;
409	  meta: Prisma.JsonValue | null;
410	};
411	
412	export type AdminAuditPage = {
413	  entries: AdminAuditEntry[];
414	  total: number;
415	};
416	
417	/**
418	 * Newest first, filtered and paginated. Both filters are served straight off
419	 * the indexes the schema already declares — `[actorId, createdAt]` and
420	 * `[action, createdAt]` — which is why those two, and not free-text search,
421	 * are the filters this page offers.
422	 */
423	export async function listAdminActions(opts: {
424	  actorId?: string;
425	  action?: AdminAction;
426	  skip?: number;
427	  take?: number;
428	}): Promise<AdminAuditPage> {
429	  const where: Prisma.AdminAuditLogWhereInput = {
430	    ...(opts.actorId ? { actorId: opts.actorId } : {}),
431	    ...(opts.action ? { action: opts.action } : {}),
432	  };
433	
434	  const [total, entries] = await Promise.all([
435	    db.adminAuditLog.count({ where }),
436	    db.adminAuditLog.findMany({
437	      where,
438	      // `id` breaks ties so paging is stable when two rows share a timestamp —
439	      // same idiom as the user list.
440	      orderBy: [{ createdAt: "desc" }, { id: "desc" }],
441	      skip: opts.skip ?? 0,
442	      take: opts.take ?? 50,
443	      select: {
444	        id: true,
445	        createdAt: true,
446	        actorId: true,
447	        actorEmail: true,
448	        action: true,
449	        targetType: true,
450	        targetId: true,
451	        meta: true,
452	      },
453	    }),
454	  ]);
455	
456	  return { entries, total };
457	}
458	
459	/**
460	 * Row count per action name, for the action filter — and, more usefully, so
461	 * the page can show which names in the vocabulary have never fired. A declared
462	 * action with zero rows means a surface that is still reading customer data
463	 * without recording it; surfacing that in the panel is how the list of owed
464	 * call sites stays visible after this change's report is forgotten.
465	 */
466	export async function countAdminActions(): Promise<Map<string, number>> {
467	  const rows = await db.adminAuditLog.groupBy({
468	    by: ["action"],
469	    _count: { _all: true },
470	  });
471	  return new Map(rows.map((r) => [r.action, r._count._all]));
472	}
473	
474	export type AdminAuditActor = { actorId: string; actorEmail: string; actions: number; lastAt: Date };
475	
476	/**
477	 * Everyone who has ever appeared in the log, for the actor filter. Grouped
478	 * rather than DISTINCT-ed because an admin who changed email address has rows
479	 * under both, and the filter should offer them once, under the newest.
480	 */
481	export async function listAdminActors(): Promise<AdminAuditActor[]> {
482	  const rows = await db.adminAuditLog.groupBy({
483	    by: ["actorId", "actorEmail"],
484	    _count: { _all: true },
485	    _max: { createdAt: true },
486	    orderBy: { _max: { createdAt: "desc" } },
487	  });
488	
489	  const seen = new Map<string, AdminAuditActor>();
490	  for (const r of rows) {
491	    const existing = seen.get(r.actorId);
492	    if (existing) {
493	      // Rows are newest-first, so the first email wins as the display name and
494	      // later ones only contribute their counts.
495	      existing.actions += r._count._all;
496	      continue;
497	    }
498	    seen.set(r.actorId, {
499	      actorId: r.actorId,
500	      actorEmail: r.actorEmail,
501	      actions: r._count._all,
502	      lastAt: r._max.createdAt ?? new Date(0),
503	    });
504	  }
505	
506	  return [...seen.values()];
507	}

---
title: revalidatePath
description: API Reference for the revalidatePath function.
related:
  links:
    - app/guides/server-actions
---

`revalidatePath` allows you to invalidate [cached data](/docs/app/getting-started/caching) on-demand for a specific path.

## Usage

`revalidatePath` can be called in Server Functions and Route Handlers.

`revalidatePath` cannot be called in Client Components or Proxy, as it only works in server environments.

> **Good to know**:
>
> - **Server Functions**: Updates the UI immediately (if viewing the affected path). Currently, it also causes all previously visited pages to refresh when navigated to again. This behavior is temporary and will be updated in the future to apply only to the specific path.
> - **Route Handlers**: Marks the path for revalidation. The revalidation is done on the next visit to the specified path. This means calling `revalidatePath` with a dynamic route segment will not immediately trigger many revalidations at once. The invalidation only happens when the path is next visited.

## Parameters

```tsx
revalidatePath(path: string, type?: 'page' | 'layout'): void;
```

- `path`: Either a string that represents your route file structure. This can be a literal path like `/product/123`, or a route pattern with dynamic segments like `/product/[slug]`. Do not append `/page` or `/layout`, use the `type` parameter instead. Must not exceed 1024 characters. This value is case-sensitive. You do not need to include a trailing slash, regardless of your [`trailingSlash`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/trailingSlash) config.
- `type`: (optional) `'page'` or `'layout'` string to change the type of path to revalidate. If `path` contains a dynamic segment, for example `/product/[slug]`, this parameter is required. If `path` is a literal path like `/product/1`, omit `type`.

Use a literal path when you want to refresh a [single page](#revalidating-a-specific-path). Use a route pattern plus `type` to refresh [all matching pages](#revalidating-a-page-path).

## Returns

`revalidatePath` does not return a value.

## What can be invalidated

The path parameter can point to pages, layouts, or route handlers:

- **Pages**: Invalidates the specific page
- **Layouts**: Invalidates the layout (the `layout.tsx` at that segment), all nested layouts beneath it, and all pages beneath them
- **Route Handlers**: Invalidates cached data accessed within route handlers. For example `revalidatePath("/api/data")` invalidates this GET handler:

```ts filename="app/api/data/route.ts"
export async function GET() {
  const data = await fetch('https://api.vercel.app/blog', {
    cache: 'force-cache',
  })

  return Response.json(await data.json())
}
```

When using [rewrites](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/rewrites), you must pass the **destination** path (the actual route file location), not the source path that appears in the browser's address bar.
